grammar.name: 一般过去时（规则动词）
grammar.zh: 已经发生的事，规则动词加 -ed：walk→walked，look→looked
grammar.ex: I looked at my desk.

grammar.name: 一般过去时（不规则动词）
grammar.zh: 常见不规则变化：eat→ate，go→went，see→saw，run→ran
grammar.ex: Benny ate my homework.

grammar.name: 过去时的否定和疑问
grammar.zh: 否定用 didn't + 动词原形，疑问用 Did … + 动词原形
grammar.ex: Did you eat my homework?

grammar.name: 一般现在时
grammar.zh: 习惯和常常发生的事，主语是第三人称单数时动词加 -s
grammar.ex: Benny eats everything.

grammar.name: There was / There were
grammar.zh: 过去"有"，单数用 was，复数用 were
grammar.ex: There was a big hole in my bag.

items.title: Benny the Goat Eats My Homework
items.zh: 山羊本尼吃了我的作业
items.summary: 汤姆家的山羊本尼什么都吃——作业、袜子、爸爸的帽子。老师不相信"山羊吃了作业"，直到本尼自己来了学校。
paras: My name is Tom. I am ten years old. I live on a small farm with my mom, my dad, my little sister Amy, and a goat. The goat's name is Benny.
Benny is white and brown. He has a short tail and two small horns. He has a long beard, like an old man. Benny is a nice goat, but he has one big problem. Benny eats everything.

He eats grass. He eats carrots. He eats apples. That is normal for a goat. But Benny also eats socks. He eats paper. He eats flowers from Mom's garden. Last summer, he ate Dad's favorite hat. Dad was very sad. He looked for the hat for two days. Then he saw a little piece of it in Benny's mouth.
"Benny!" Dad said. "That was my lucky hat!"
Benny looked at Dad. He chewed and chewed. He did not say sorry. Goats never say sorry.

Every morning, I walk to the yard and give Benny his breakfast. I give him hay and one carrot. He eats the hay. He eats the carrot. Then he looks at me with his big yellow eyes. He wants more. He always wants more.

One Monday morning, I had a big problem. I had my math homework in my bag. It was a lot of homework. I worked on it for three hours on Sunday night. I did twenty math problems. I checked every answer two times. I was very proud of it.
I put my bag next to the door of the barn. Then I gave Benny his breakfast. I talked to him for a minute. I said, "Benny, today I have a math test. Wish me luck."
Benny did not wish me luck. Benny was busy.
I turned around and looked at my bag. There was a big hole in my bag. There were little pieces of paper on the ground. And there was a goat with paper in his mouth.
"Benny!" I shouted. "No! Did you eat my homework?"

Benny chewed. He looked very happy. I looked into my bag. My pencils were there. My lunch was there. My math book was there. But my homework was not there. Benny ate my homework. He ate all twenty problems.
I ran into the house. "Mom! Dad! Benny ate my homework!"
Mom laughed. Dad laughed. Amy laughed so hard that she fell off her chair.
"It is not funny," I said. "My teacher will not believe me. Nobody believes that story. It is the oldest story in the world."
Dad stopped laughing. "You are right," he said. "Teachers hear that story every year. But usually it is a dog, not a goat."
I walked to school that day. I was very worried. My teacher is Mrs. Park. She is kind, but she is very strict about homework. She always says, "Homework is important. No homework, no recess."
I sat at my desk. I looked at my desk. I looked at the window. I did not want to talk to Mrs. Park. But she walked to me.
"Tom," she said. "Where is your homework?"
"My goat ate it," I said.
The class was very quiet. Then everybody laughed. A boy named Jake laughed the loudest. "A goat!" he said. "Tom has a homework-eating goat!"
Mrs. Park did not laugh. She looked at me over her glasses. "Tom," she said, "that is a very old story. I did not believe it last year, and I do not believe it this year."
"But it is true!" I said. "His name is Benny. He eats everything. He ate my dad's hat!"
"Hmm," said Mrs. Park. "No homework, no recess. You can do the homework again during recess."
I was very sad. I liked recess. Recess is the best part of the day. I sat in the classroom and did my math problems again. I did not finish all of them. I was hungry and tired.
Then something strange happened.
At eleven o'clock, we heard a noise in the hallway. It was a funny noise. It sounded like "Meh-eh-eh-eh!"
Mrs. Park stopped. "What was that?" she asked.
"Meh-eh-eh-eh!" said the noise again. It was closer now.
The door of our classroom opened. And there, in the door, was Benny.
He had a piece of rope around his neck. The rope was chewed in the middle. He walked to school by himself! He followed my smell all the way from the farm. That is two miles!
Everybody screamed. Then everybody laughed. Benny walked into the classroom like a king. He looked at the children. He looked at the desks. Then he looked at Mrs. Park's desk.
On Mrs. Park's desk, there was a big pile of paper. It was our spelling homework. There were twenty-five pages.
"Oh no," I said. "Benny, no!"
Benny walked to the desk. He took one page in his mouth. He chewed it. He took another page. He chewed that one too. He looked very happy.
"Stop him!" said Mrs. Park. "That is the spelling homework!"

Jake ran to Benny. Benny jumped on a chair. Jake ran around the chair. Benny jumped on a table. Two girls ran to the table. Benny jumped down and ran under Mrs. Park's desk. He had three more pages in his mouth.
The principal, Mr. Lopez, heard the noise. He came into the classroom. "What is going on here?" he asked. Then he saw Benny. Benny saw Mr. Lopez. Mr. Lopez had a sandwich in his hand.
Benny walked out from under the desk. He walked to Mr. Lopez. He looked at the sandwich. Mr. Lopez looked at Benny.
"Do not give him the sandwich," I said. "He will follow you forever."
It was too late. Benny ate the sandwich. Then he ate the paper bag. Then he started to eat Mr. Lopez's tie.
Finally, I took the rope. "Come on, Benny," I said. "Time to go home." Benny followed me. He was full and happy. He did not want to eat anything more. For a goat, that is a big surprise.

Mrs. Park looked at her empty desk. There was no more spelling homework. There were only a few small pieces of paper. She looked at me. Then she started to laugh. She laughed and laughed. She laughed so much that she needed to sit down.
"Tom," she said, "I am sorry. Your story was true. Your goat really eats homework."
"I told you," I said.
"You did," she said. "And you can have recess tomorrow. Also, class, there is good news. Your spelling homework is gone. You do not need to give it to me this week."
Everybody cheered. Jake cheered the loudest. "Benny is the best goat in the world!" he shouted.
That afternoon, my dad came to school with the truck. We put Benny in the back. Benny looked out of the truck like a happy dog. All the children waved goodbye. Benny said "Meh-eh-eh!" to everybody.

Now Benny is famous at my school. The children draw pictures of him. Mrs. Park has a new rule. The rule is on the classroom wall. It says, "No goats in the classroom." Under the rule, there is a small picture of Benny.

And me? I have a new rule too. Every morning, I give Benny his breakfast. But I never put my bag next to the barn. I put my bag in the house, on a high shelf, far away from my best friend, the hungry goat.

grammar.name: 现在进行时
grammar.zh: 正在发生的事：am / is / are + 动词-ing
grammar.ex: Mr. Sweep is cleaning the cat's food.

grammar.name: can / can't 表示能力
grammar.zh: can + 动词原形，否定 can't
grammar.ex: It can talk, but it can't listen.

grammar.name: 一般现在时与现在进行时对比
grammar.zh: 平常习惯用一般现在时，此刻正在做用进行时
grammar.ex: Usually the cat sleeps on the sofa. Right now, she is sitting on the fridge.

grammar.name: 祈使句
grammar.zh: 用动词原形开头，表示命令或请求；否定用 Don't
grammar.ex: Don't clean the cat!

grammar.name: want to / like + -ing
grammar.zh: want to + 动词原形；like + 动词-ing 表示喜欢做
grammar.ex: He likes watching TV.

items.title: Grandpa's Robot Is Cleaning Everything
items.zh: 爷爷的机器人在打扫一切
items.summary: 爷爷买了一个会说话的扫地机器人"大扫"。它太爱干净了：扫走了猫粮、拖走了爷爷的拖鞋，最后连猫都想"清理掉"。
paras: My grandpa is seventy-five years old. He has white hair, big glasses, and a very loud laugh. He likes watching TV. He likes eating cookies. He does not like cleaning. Grandpa says, "Cleaning is boring. I want a robot to do it."

Last week, Grandpa got his wish. A big box came to his house. Inside the box, there was a round robot. It was black and silver. It had one blue light on top, like an eye. It had two small brushes under it.
"This is a robot vacuum," Grandpa said. "It can clean the floor by itself. It can talk too. Listen!" He pushed a button.
The robot made a happy sound. "Beep boop! Hello! My name is Mr. Sweep. I love clean floors. Clean floors make me happy. Where is the dirt?"
I laughed. "Grandpa, it talks like a game show!"
"Yes," said Grandpa. "And it never gets tired. Now I can watch TV all day."
Grandpa sat on the sofa. He turned on the TV. Mr. Sweep started to work.
Mr. Sweep is very fast. He goes under the table. He goes under the chairs. He goes into every corner. He makes a little noise, like a bee. "Bzzzzz. Bzzzzz. Dirt found! Dirt removed!"

At first, everything was wonderful. The kitchen floor was clean. The hallway floor was clean. There were no crumbs under the table. Grandpa was very happy. "Look!" he said. "I am not cleaning, but the house is cleaning itself!"
But Mr. Sweep had a problem. He loved cleaning too much.
Now it is Saturday morning. I am visiting Grandpa again. I am standing in the kitchen, and I am watching Mr. Sweep. Mr. Sweep is not cleaning the floor. Mr. Sweep is cleaning the cat's food.
"Stop!" I say. "That is not dirt! That is breakfast!"
"Beep boop!" says Mr. Sweep. "Small brown things found. Small brown things removed!"

The cat's bowl is empty now. The cat, Pepper, is looking at the robot. She is not happy. Pepper is a big gray cat. Usually the cat sleeps on the sofa. Right now, she is sitting on the fridge. She is watching Mr. Sweep with angry green eyes.
"Grandpa!" I call. "Your robot is eating Pepper's food!"
Grandpa is in the living room. He is wearing his favorite blue slippers. He is eating a cookie and watching a cooking show. "Don't worry," he says. "Mr. Sweep is smart. He knows the difference."
Mr. Sweep does not know the difference.

Mr. Sweep rolls into the living room. "Beep boop! Crumbs detected!" He goes straight to Grandpa's feet. Grandpa has cookie crumbs on his slippers. Mr. Sweep pushes his brushes against the slippers. Bzzzzz!
"Hey!" says Grandpa. "Those are my feet!"
"Large dirty object found," says Mr. Sweep. Then he does something terrible. He grabs one blue slipper with his brushes, and he pulls it. He is pulling the slipper off Grandpa's foot!
"Let go!" shouts Grandpa. He pulls his foot back. Mr. Sweep pulls the slipper. Grandpa pulls his foot. It is like a game of tug of war. A seventy-five-year-old man and a little round robot.
Mr. Sweep wins. The slipper comes off. Mr. Sweep spins around three times and rolls away very fast with the slipper. "Beep boop! Slipper removed! House is cleaner!"
Grandpa looks at his one bare foot. Then he looks at me. "Get my slipper back," he says.

I run after the robot. Mr. Sweep goes under the sofa. I get down on the floor. I am looking under the sofa. It is dark. I can see the blue light. I can see the slipper. I can also see two old socks, a TV remote, and a cookie. Mr. Sweep is collecting things!
"Mr. Sweep, come out!" I say.
"Beep boop. I am resting," says Mr. Sweep. "Cleaning is hard work."
Grandpa laughs his big, loud laugh. "Ha! Now he says cleaning is hard work!"
I pull out the slipper, the socks, the remote, and the cookie. Grandpa is very happy to see the remote. "I was looking for that for two days!" he says.
Then something happens. Pepper the cat jumps down from the fridge. She is very brave. She walks to the sofa. She wants her breakfast back. She sits in front of the sofa and looks at the blue light.
Mr. Sweep rolls out. He sees Pepper. He stops. His blue light goes on and off, on and off.
"Beep boop," he says slowly. "Very large dust ball found."
"Oh no," I say. "Pepper is not a dust ball!"
"Large gray fuzzy dust ball," says Mr. Sweep. "Cleaning now!"
Mr. Sweep rolls toward Pepper. Pepper's tail gets big, like a bottle brush. Her back goes up. She makes a very angry sound. "HISSSSS!"
Mr. Sweep does not stop. Robots are not afraid of cats.
"Don't clean the cat!" Grandpa shouts. He jumps up from the sofa. He has one slipper on and one slipper in his hand. He is running across the living room. "Don't clean the cat!"

Pepper jumps. She does not run away. She jumps on top of Mr. Sweep! Now the cat is sitting on the robot, and the robot is driving around the living room. Around the sofa. Around the table. Into the kitchen and back again. Pepper is holding on with all her claws. She looks surprised. Then she looks happy. She is riding the robot like a little gray cowboy.
"Beep boop! Heavy dust! Heavy dust!" says Mr. Sweep. He spins in a circle. Pepper spins too.

My little brother, Leo, comes in from the garden. He sees the cat riding the robot. His mouth opens very wide. "That is the coolest thing in the world!" he says. He takes out Mom's phone and makes a video.

Finally, Mr. Sweep's battery is low. He says, "Beep. Battery low. Going home." He rolls slowly back to his charging station in the corner. Pepper is still on top of him. She does not want to get off. Mr. Sweep stops. The blue light goes off. Pepper lies down on top of the warm robot, and she goes to sleep.
Grandpa sits down on the sofa. He is tired. I am tired. Even the robot is tired. Only Pepper is happy. She is sleeping on her new, warm bed.
"Well," says Grandpa. "That robot can clean the floor. But it can't tell a cat from a dust ball. It can talk, but it can't listen."
"Are you going to send it back?" I ask.

Grandpa looks at Pepper. She is purring on top of Mr. Sweep. Then he looks at Leo's video. In the video, a cat is riding a robot around the kitchen, and an old man is running behind them with one slipper.
Grandpa starts to laugh. "No," he says. "I am keeping it. This is the best TV show in the house."

Now every Saturday, Grandpa does something new. He puts his slippers on a high shelf. He puts the cat food on the counter. Then he pushes the button. Mr. Sweep says, "Beep boop! Hello! Where is the dirt?" And Pepper jumps on top, ready for her ride.

grammar.name: 形容词比较级
grammar.zh: 两者比较：短词加 -er（big→bigger），长词用 more（more beautiful），后面接 than
grammar.ex: It was bigger than our table.

grammar.name: 形容词最高级
grammar.zh: 三者以上比较：the + -est（the biggest），或 the most + 形容词
grammar.ex: This is definitely the biggest pancake.

grammar.name: 不规则比较级
grammar.zh: good→better→best，bad→worse→worst
grammar.ex: Mrs. Brown's pancake is better.

grammar.name: as … as
grammar.zh: 两者一样：as + 形容词原级 + as
grammar.ex: It was about as big as a dinner plate.

grammar.name: too + 形容词
grammar.zh: 太……（以至于不能）
grammar.ex: The pan is too small.

items.title: The Biggest Pancake in Town
items.summary: 小镇举办煎饼比赛，莉莉和爸爸想做"全镇最大的煎饼"。煎饼越做越大，最后大到要用梯子翻面。
paras: Every spring, my town has a pancake contest. It is in the park, next to the lake. People come from everywhere. They bring their best pans, their best flour, and their best ideas. There are three prizes. There is a prize for the most delicious pancake. There is a prize for the most beautiful pancake. And there is a prize for the biggest pancake.
My name is Lily. I am nine years old. This year, my dad and I wanted to win the prize for the biggest pancake.
"Last year, the biggest pancake was as big as a car wheel," said Dad. "This year, we are going to make a pancake bigger than a car wheel. Bigger than a table. Bigger than a door!"
"Bigger than our house?" I asked.
Dad thought about it. "Maybe not that big," he said.

We started on Friday night. We went to the store. We bought ten bags of flour, sixty eggs, and twenty big bottles of milk. The woman at the store looked at our cart. "Are you feeding an army?" she asked.
"No," I said. "We are making the biggest pancake in town."
She laughed. "Good luck. Mrs. Brown is in the contest again. Her pancakes are always the best."

Mrs. Brown lives on our street. She is seventy years old, and she is a great cook. Her pancakes are softer than clouds. Her pancakes are sweeter than candy. Last year she won two prizes. Dad says she is the best cook in the whole state.

On Saturday morning, we went to the park. There were many tables, many pans, and many people. It smelled wonderful. There was butter and syrup everywhere. A big sign said, "Pancake Contest! Judges at 12 o'clock!"
Mrs. Brown was at the table next to us. She had a small pan and a small bowl. She smiled at us. "Hello, Lily," she said. "What are you making today?"
"The biggest pancake in town," I said proudly.
She looked at our bags of flour and our sixty eggs. "My goodness," she said. "Your pan needs to be very big."
Dad stopped. He looked at our pan. It was our normal kitchen pan. It was round and black. It was about as big as a dinner plate.
"Oh no," said Dad. "The pan is too small."

We had flour. We had eggs. We had milk. But we did not have a big pan. Dad looked around the park. He looked at the trees. He looked at the lake. Then he looked at a big metal sign. It said, "Please Do Not Feed the Ducks."
"Lily," said Dad, "I have an idea."

Ten minutes later, we had the sign. A park worker gave it to us. He thought it was very funny. The sign was flat, metal, and very big. It was bigger than our table. It was as long as a bed. Dad put it on top of four camping stoves. "Our new pan!" he said.

Then we mixed the batter. We used a big plastic bucket. We put in the flour. We put in the eggs. We put in the milk. We mixed and mixed. My arms got tired. Dad's arms got tired. A crowd started to watch us. Some children helped us mix.

"Pour it!" said Dad. We poured the batter on the hot sign. It was a big white lake on the metal. It went from one end to the other end. It covered the words "Do Not Feed the Ducks." The crowd cheered.
The pancake started to cook. It made a happy sound. Tssssss. It smelled very good. Little bubbles came up on top. "When there are bubbles, it is time to flip it," said Dad.
Then we had a new problem. How do you flip a pancake as big as a bed?
Dad tried with our kitchen spatula. It was too small. It looked like a spoon next to an elephant. I tried with two spatulas. That did not work either. The pancake was too heavy.
"It is going to burn!" said a boy in the crowd.

Mrs. Brown walked over from her table. She looked at the pancake. She looked at us. Then she smiled. "You need more hands," she said. She turned to the crowd. "Everybody, come here! We are going to flip a giant pancake!"

Twenty people came. They stood around the sign. Each person took two spatulas or two big spoons. A man from the fire station brought a ladder. Dad climbed up the ladder. He was higher than everyone. He was the captain.
"On three!" Dad shouted. "One... two... THREE!"
Everybody lifted at the same time. The giant pancake went up into the air. It flew higher than the people. For one second, it was like a big golden blanket in the sky. Everybody was quiet.
Then it came down. FLOP!
It landed on the sign, brown side up. It was perfect. Well, almost perfect. One small corner landed on Dad's head. He looked like he was wearing a pancake hat.

The crowd went crazy. They cheered and clapped. Some people took pictures. The ducks from the lake came to look too. They were very interested. Remember, the sign said, "Do Not Feed the Ducks." Now the sign was under a pancake, and nobody could read it.

At twelve o'clock, the judges came. There were three judges. They had clipboards and serious faces. They looked at Mrs. Brown's pancakes first. They were small, round, and golden. They tasted them. "Mmm," said the first judge. "These are the most delicious pancakes I have ever eaten."
Then they came to our table. They looked at our pancake. They looked at the ladder. They looked at Dad. He still had a little pancake on his head.
"Well," said the second judge. "This is definitely the biggest pancake. It is bigger than my car."
"Is it good?" asked the third judge. She took a small piece and tasted it. She thought for a long time. "It is... not bad," she said. "Mrs. Brown's pancake is better. But yours is the funniest."

We won the prize for the biggest pancake! It was a gold medal with a little picture of a pancake on it. Mrs. Brown won the prize for the most delicious pancake. And the prize for the most beautiful pancake? It went to a little boy who made a pancake shaped like a duck.

After the contest, we did not know what to do with our giant pancake. It was too big to take home. So we shared it. Everybody in the park had a piece. We put butter and syrup on it. People ate pancake for one hour. Mrs. Brown said, "Your pancake is not as soft as mine. But it is the friendliest pancake in town."
That night, I asked Dad, "Next year, can we make a bigger pancake?"
Dad looked at his sore arms. He looked at the pancake batter in his hair. "Next year," he said, "let's make the smallest pancake in town."

grammar.name: be going to 表示计划
grammar.zh: 已经打算好的事：am/is/are going to + 动词原形
grammar.ex: I am going to cook dinner every night.

grammar.name: will 表示临时决定或预测
grammar.zh: 说话时才决定的事，或对将来的猜测：will + 动词原形
grammar.ex: I will call the pizza shop.

grammar.name: 一般将来时的疑问
grammar.zh: Are you going to …? / Will you …?
grammar.ex: are you going to cook spaghetti again?

grammar.name: 时间顺序词
grammar.zh: first, then, next, after that, finally 帮助讲清楚先后顺序
grammar.ex: First, he put on Mom's apron.

grammar.name: must / have to
grammar.zh: 必须：must + 动词原形；have to 更口语，表示外部要求
grammar.ex: You must not open the pot!

items.title: Dad Is Going to Be a Chef
items.summary: 妈妈出差一周，爸爸宣布"我要当大厨"。他的计划很宏伟，结果每天都出状况：蓝色的意面、会爆炸的爆米花，还有一个惊喜的结局。
paras: On Sunday night, Mom packed her suitcase. She was going to Chicago for work. "I am going to be away for one week," she said. "Seven days. Can you three be okay without me?"
"Of course," said Dad. He stood up and put his hands on his hips. "While you are away, I am going to cook dinner every night. Real dinner. Not pizza. I am going to be a chef!"
My sister Mia and I looked at each other. Dad can make toast. Dad can make coffee. Once, he made a sandwich with peanut butter and pickles. That was the end of his cooking.
Mom looked at Dad for a long time. "Okay," she said slowly. "The recipes are in the blue book in the kitchen. The fire extinguisher is under the sink."
"Ha ha," said Dad. "Very funny."

On Monday, Dad came home early. He was very excited. He had three bags of food. "Tonight," he said, "we are going to have spaghetti with tomato sauce. It is going to be the best spaghetti in the world."

First, he put on Mom's apron. It was pink with little yellow flowers. Then he opened the blue recipe book. Next, he filled the biggest pot with water. After that, he looked at the recipe for a long time.
"It says one teaspoon of salt," he said. "But I am a chef. Chefs do not measure. Chefs feel."
He put in a lot of salt. Then he felt something else. He put in some blue food coloring. "For fun," he said.
Finally, dinner was ready. The spaghetti was blue. Bright blue. The sauce was red. Together, they looked like a sad clown.
"It is a new style," said Dad. "Everybody is going to love it."
Mia tasted it. I tasted it. It was very, very salty. It tasted like the ocean. Mia drank three glasses of water.
"Dad," said Mia, "are you going to cook spaghetti again?"
"No," said Dad. "Tomorrow I am going to make something different."

On Tuesday, Dad made soup. He put in every vegetable in the fridge. Carrots, potatoes, onions, broccoli, and one very old cucumber. He also put in some leftover pancakes. "Nothing goes to waste in my kitchen," he said. The soup was brown and thick. It was so thick that the spoon stood up in the middle of the bowl. Mia called it "soup cement."

On Wednesday, Dad made fish. He put the fish in the oven. Then he watched a soccer game on TV. He forgot the fish. After one hour, the smoke alarm started to scream. BEEP! BEEP! BEEP! The kitchen was full of gray smoke. Dad ran into the kitchen. He opened all the windows. He waved a towel at the alarm. Our dog, Biscuit, ran around and barked at the smoke.
The fish was black. It was as hard as a rock. Dad looked at it. "I think," he said, "this fish is extra crispy."
"Dad," I said, "I will call the pizza shop."
"No!" said Dad. "No pizza! I made a promise. I am a chef!"
We ate cereal for dinner. Dad ate cereal too. He looked tired.
On Thursday, Mom called us on video. "How is everything?" she asked. "How is the cooking?"
Dad smiled a big smile. "Wonderful," he said. "Every dinner is an adventure."
Behind him, Mia held up a piece of paper. It said, "HELP." Mom laughed so hard that she had to put the phone down.
On Friday, Dad decided to make dessert. "Everybody likes dessert," he said. "Tonight we are going to have popcorn and chocolate cake."

The popcorn came first. Dad did not use the small popcorn bags. He used a big bag of popcorn seeds and a big pot. He put in one cup of seeds. Then he thought, "More is better." He put in the whole bag. He put the lid on the pot. He turned the fire to high.
"Dad," I said, "I think that is too much."
"Trust the chef," said Dad.
For one minute, nothing happened. Then we heard it. Pop. Pop, pop. Pop, pop, pop, pop! POP-POP-POP-POP-POP!
The lid started to move. It went up, and it came down. It went up higher. Popcorn came out from under it.
"You must not open the pot!" Dad shouted. "Hold the lid!"

Mia held the lid with a big spoon. I held it with a towel. Dad held it with his hands. The popcorn did not care. BANG! The lid flew up to the ceiling. Popcorn exploded all over the kitchen like white snow. It was on the floor. It was on the table. It was in the sink. It was on top of the fridge. Some of it was in Dad's hair.
Biscuit was the happiest dog in the world. He ran around and ate popcorn from the floor. He ate so much that he lay down on his back and did not move.
We stood in the kitchen. We were covered in popcorn. Then Mia started to laugh. I started to laugh. Finally, Dad laughed too. We laughed until our stomachs hurt.
"Okay," said Dad. "No chocolate cake tonight. We have to clean the kitchen."
On Saturday, Dad did something different. He did not cook alone. He said, "Today, we are going to cook together. And we are going to follow the recipe. Exactly."

He gave Mia the measuring cups. He gave me the eggs. He read the recipe out loud, slowly. "One cup of flour. Two eggs. Half a cup of sugar." We did everything carefully. We made a simple chicken with rice and green beans. We made a small chocolate cake. Nothing was blue. Nothing exploded. Nothing went black.
It was delicious. Really delicious. Dad was so proud. He took a picture of his plate and sent it to Mom.

On Sunday afternoon, Mom came home. She opened the front door. She smelled the air. "Something smells good," she said. She walked into the kitchen. The table was ready. There was chicken, rice, and the second chocolate cake of the week.
"Who made this?" she asked.
"The chefs," said Dad. He pointed at Mia and me. "All three of us."
Mom tasted the chicken. "This is very good," she said. Then she looked up. She saw something on top of the kitchen cupboard. It was a little piece of popcorn. She looked at Dad. "What is that?"
Dad smiled. "That," he said, "is a long story. And I am going to tell you everything. But first, have some cake."

items.title: The Raccoon at Our Picnic
items.summary: 一家人去公园野餐，一只聪明的浣熊一次又一次偷走他们的食物。全家想尽办法，最后发现浣熊还带来了全家人。
paras: Last Sunday was a beautiful day. The sun was warm, and the sky was blue. My mom said, "Let's have a picnic!" So we went to Green Lake Park. My mom, my dad, my brother Sam, my grandma, and me. My name is Rosa.

We had a big picnic basket and a red cooler. In the basket, there were sandwiches, peaches, and two boxes of cookies. In the cooler, there were cold drinks and a big bowl of potato salad. Grandma made the potato salad. It is her famous recipe. Nobody can make it like Grandma.

We found a nice place under a big tree. There was a wooden table next to the tree and a small river behind it. Dad put the blanket on the grass. Mom put the basket on the table. Grandma sat on a chair in the shade. Sam and I ran to the river to look for fish.
When we came back, Dad looked confused. "Where are the sandwiches?" he asked.
"They are in the basket," said Mom.
Dad looked in the basket. "No, they are not."
We looked everywhere. We looked on the table. We looked under the table. We looked in the cooler. We looked behind Grandma's chair. The sandwiches were not there.
"Maybe we forgot them at home," said Mom.
"No," said Sam. "I saw them in the car." Sam is seven. He remembers every food he sees.

Then I saw something. There were small footprints on the table. They looked like little hands. And there was a piece of bread on the grass. Then another piece. The pieces of bread made a line. The line went to the big tree.

I looked up. On a branch, there was a raccoon. It was fat and gray. It had a black mask around its eyes, like a little robber. It had a striped tail. And in its paws, there was a sandwich. Our sandwich!
"Look!" I shouted. "A raccoon! It took our sandwiches!"
The raccoon looked at me. It did not run away. It ate the sandwich slowly. It looked very happy. Then it washed its paws in the air. Raccoons do that. They look very polite, but they are thieves.

"Well," said Dad, "we still have the peaches and the cookies. Let's keep them safe." He put the peaches and cookies in the cooler and closed the lid. "There," he said. "Now the raccoon can't get them."
We played a game with a ball. We laughed and ran. After twenty minutes, we were hungry again. Dad opened the cooler. He looked inside. He looked at us. His face was funny.
"The cookies are gone," he said.
"What? But you closed the lid!" said Mom.
"I know," said Dad. "That raccoon is clever. It opened the cooler."
Sam was very sad. "Not the cookies," he said. "Is there any food left?"
"We still have some peaches," said Grandma. "And my potato salad. The raccoon did not take the potato salad."
We looked at the tree again. Now there were two raccoons on the branch. The first raccoon had a cookie. The second raccoon had a cookie too. They looked down at us. I think they were laughing.
"Okay," said Dad. "This is war. We need a plan."

Dad's plan was this. He put the cooler on the table. He put Grandma's chair next to the cooler. Then he put a heavy rock on top of the lid. "Now nobody can open it," he said. "Not even a clever raccoon."
Mom had a plan too. She put the peaches in a plastic bag and hung the bag high on a pole. "Raccoons can't fly," she said.
Sam had a plan. He sat on the blanket with a big stick and watched the tree. "I am the guard," he said. Two minutes later, he was asleep.
I had a plan too. I did not tell anyone. I took one peach and put it on the grass far away from our table. Then I hid behind a bush and waited. I wanted to see the raccoons.
I waited and waited. Then the bushes moved. A raccoon came out. It was the fat one. It picked up the peach. It smelled it. But it did not eat it. It made a little sound. "Chrrr, chrrr."

And then the bushes moved again. Out came another raccoon. And another. And another. And then, very slowly, three baby raccoons. They were small and fluffy. They walked behind their mother in a line, like little soldiers.

I counted them. There are six raccoons in the tree, I thought. No, wait. More! There were raccoons in the tree, raccoons under the table, and raccoons in the bushes. It was a raccoon family party, and our picnic was the food.
I ran back to my family. "Mom! Dad! There are not two raccoons. There are ten!"

But it was too late. While Dad was looking at the cooler and Mom was looking at the peaches, a big raccoon was on the table. It was holding Grandma's bowl of potato salad. Grandma's famous potato salad!

Grandma stood up from her chair. She is eighty years old, but she is fast. "Oh no, you don't!" she said. She took her big straw hat and waved it at the raccoon. "That is my potato salad! I made that!"
The raccoon looked at Grandma. Grandma looked at the raccoon. Nobody moved. It was like a cowboy movie.
Then the raccoon did something surprising. It put the bowl down. It pushed the bowl back to Grandma with its little paws. Then it walked away.
We were all very quiet. Then Dad said, "Grandma, I think the raccoons are afraid of you."
"Good," said Grandma. She sat down and held her bowl. "Nobody steals my potato salad."

In the end, we did not have sandwiches. We did not have cookies. We had only a few peaches and a big bowl of potato salad. We ate it all together on the blanket. It was the best potato salad in the world. Even Sam said so, and he does not like potatoes.
When we walked to the car, I looked back at the tree. The raccoon family was sitting on the branches. The baby raccoons were eating the last cookies. The fat raccoon was looking at us.
I waved. "Goodbye, raccoons!"
Now, when we go on picnics, we have new rules. We do not sit under trees. We keep the food in the car. And we always bring Grandma. She is the best raccoon guard in the world.

grammar.name: 一般现在时（日常习惯）
grammar.zh: 每天都做的事用一般现在时，he/she/it 后动词加 -s 或 -es
grammar.ex: My mom gets up at six o'clock.

grammar.name: 频率副词
grammar.zh: always 总是，usually 通常，often 经常，sometimes 有时，never 从不；放在 be 动词之后、实义动词之前

grammar.zh: at + 钟点，in + 早上/下午/月份，on + 星期几/日期

items.title: My Day from Morning to Night
items.summary: 用一天的生活把最常用的动词、时间词和频率副词串起来：起床、刷牙、上学、吃饭、做作业、睡觉。每段都在重复使用高频词。
paras: Hello! My name is Sara. I am eleven years old. I live in a small house with my mom, my dad, my brother Ben, and our cat, Lucky. Today I want to tell you about my day. My day is very busy. It starts early in the morning, and it ends late at night. Let me show you what I do every day.
In the morning
My mom gets up at six o'clock. She is always the first person in our house to get up. She makes coffee, and she opens all the windows. She likes fresh air in the morning.

I wake up at half past six. My clock makes a loud noise. "Ring, ring, ring!" I never like that sound. I usually stay in bed for five more minutes. I close my eyes and think, "Five more minutes, just five more minutes." Then my mom calls me. "Sara! Get up! It is time for school!" So I get up.

First, I go to the bathroom. I wash my face with cold water. Cold water helps me wake up. Then I brush my teeth. I brush them for two minutes. My dentist says two minutes is the right time. I use a pink toothbrush. Ben uses a blue one. Sometimes he uses my toothbrush by mistake, and I get very angry.

After that, I go back to my room and get dressed. On Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, I wear my school sweater. On Tuesday and Thursday, I wear my sports clothes, because I have a PE class. I comb my hair and put it in a ponytail. I always check my bag. I put in my books, my pencil case, my water bottle, and my homework.

At seven o'clock, I have breakfast. I usually eat a bowl of cereal with milk and a banana. Sometimes I eat toast with butter and jam. On cold days, my mom makes hot oatmeal. Ben often eats two bowls of cereal. He is always hungry. My dad doesn't eat breakfast at home. He drinks a cup of coffee very fast and runs out of the door. He eats a sandwich on the train.
Lucky eats breakfast too. She eats cat food from a small red bowl. She always meows at me in the morning. I think she says, "Good morning, Sara! Where is my food?"
Going to school

At half past seven, I leave home. I usually walk to school with my brother. The school is not far. It is about fifteen minutes on foot. On rainy days, my dad drives us, or we take the bus. The bus stop is at the end of our street. The bus is often late, so we wait under an umbrella.

On the way to school, we see many things. We see the bakery. It smells like fresh bread. We see the park with big green trees. We see Mr. Green, our neighbor. He walks his dog every morning. His dog is big and white, and it is very friendly. We always say, "Good morning, Mr. Green!" and he always says, "Good morning, kids! Have a good day!"
At school
School starts at eight o'clock. I am never late, because my teacher does not like it. My teacher's name is Ms. Hill. She is tall and kind, and she has a big smile.

In the morning, we have three classes. On Monday, we have English, math, and science. English is my favorite subject. I like reading stories and writing new words. Math is sometimes difficult for me. I am good at adding numbers, but I am not good at dividing. Science is fun. We often do small experiments. Last week, we made a volcano with baking soda and vinegar.
At ten o'clock, we have a short break. It is twenty minutes long. We go out to the playground. My friends and I play games or talk. Sometimes we eat a small snack, like an apple or some crackers.

At twelve o'clock, we have lunch. I usually eat lunch at school. I bring my lunch from home in a lunch box. My favorite lunch is a cheese sandwich, some carrots, and a cookie. My friend Amy always brings rice and chicken. Sometimes we share our food. After lunch, we go out and play again. We play soccer, or we jump rope.

In the afternoon, we have two more classes. On Monday afternoon, we have music and art. In music class, we sing songs and play the drums. In art class, we draw and paint. I love art class. Last month, I painted a picture of Lucky. Now it is on the wall in our kitchen.
School finishes at three o'clock. The bell rings, and everybody runs to the door. Everybody is happy at three o'clock.
After school
I get home at half past three. I am usually hungry, so I have a snack. I often eat some fruit or a yogurt. Then I rest for a few minutes. I sit on the sofa with Lucky. She likes to sit on my legs.

At four o'clock, I do my homework. I do not like homework very much, but I always do it. My mom says, "Homework first, games later." I sit at the kitchen table. I usually have math homework and English homework. Sometimes I have a science project. If I have a question, I ask my mom. If my mom does not know, I ask Ben. He is thirteen, and he is very smart. But sometimes he says, "Do it yourself!"

After my homework, I have free time. On Tuesday and Thursday, I have piano lessons. My piano teacher comes to our house at five o'clock. The lesson is one hour long. I practice for twenty minutes every day. On other days, I play outside with my friends. We ride our bikes or play in the park. Sometimes I read a book in my room. I love books about animals and adventures.
In the evening
My dad comes home at six o'clock. He is often tired after work, but he always smiles when he sees us. He asks, "How was school today?" And I tell him everything.

At half past six, we cook dinner together. On Monday, my dad cooks. On Tuesday, my mom cooks. On Wednesday, Ben and I help. We make pasta or tacos. I wash the vegetables, and Ben cuts them. I am not allowed to use the big knife yet.

At seven o'clock, we have dinner. We always eat dinner together at the table. We do not watch TV during dinner. We talk about our day. My mom tells us about her job. She is a nurse. My dad tells us funny stories about his office. Ben talks about soccer. And I talk about my friends and my teacher. Dinner is my favorite time of the day, because everybody is together.
After dinner, we clean the kitchen. I put the dishes on the counter. Ben washes them. My dad dries them. My mom puts the food in the fridge. Lucky watches us. She waits for a little piece of chicken.
At eight o'clock, I have some more free time. Sometimes I watch TV for thirty minutes. Sometimes I play a board game with my family. On Friday night, we often watch a movie together and eat popcorn.
At night
At half past eight, I take a shower. Then I put on my pajamas. My pajamas are yellow with little stars on them. I brush my teeth again. I always brush my teeth in the morning and at night.

At nine o'clock, I go to bed. My mom comes to my room and reads me a story. I am eleven, and I can read by myself, but I still like it when she reads to me. Then she turns off the light and says, "Good night, Sara. Sleep well." I say, "Good night, Mom."
Lucky often comes into my room at night. She jumps on my bed and sleeps next to my feet. She is warm and soft. Sometimes I dream about her. In my dream, she can talk.
Weekends are different

On Saturday, I do not go to school. I get up late, at eight o'clock or even nine o'clock. We have a big breakfast with pancakes. In the afternoon, we often go to the park or visit my grandma. My grandma lives in a small town near the sea. She always makes cookies for us.

On Sunday, we clean the house in the morning. I clean my room and make my bed. In the afternoon, I see my friends, or we go swimming. On Sunday night, I go to bed early, because on Monday everything starts again.
My family's days
My family's days are different from my day. Let me tell you about them.

My mom is a nurse. She works at a big hospital in the city. Some weeks, she works in the day. Other weeks, she works at night. When she works at night, she leaves home at seven o'clock in the evening, and she comes back at seven o'clock in the morning. Then she sleeps all day. We must be very quiet in the house. Ben and I walk on our toes, and we never play loud music. My mom says her job is hard, but she loves it. She helps sick people every day.

My dad works in an office. He starts work at nine o'clock and finishes at five o'clock. He takes the train to the city. The train ride is forty minutes long. He reads the news on his phone, or he sleeps a little. At lunch time, he usually eats with his friends from work. On Friday, he sometimes works from home. Then he sits at the kitchen table with his computer, and Lucky sits on his keyboard. He says Lucky is his new boss.

My brother Ben goes to a different school. It is a middle school, and it is bigger than my school. He takes the bus every morning at seven o'clock, so he gets up before me. He has a lot of homework every day. After school, he plays soccer with his team. They practice on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. On Saturday morning, they have a game. We often go and watch him. He is a fast runner, and he sometimes scores a goal. When he scores, my dad jumps and shouts very loudly. Ben says it is embarrassing, but I think he likes it.

And Lucky? Lucky has the easiest day of all. She sleeps in the morning. She eats at noon. She sleeps in the afternoon. She looks out of the window at the birds. She sleeps again in the evening. At night, she runs around the house very fast for no reason. Then she sleeps on my bed. I think Lucky sleeps for sixteen hours every day. Sometimes I want to be a cat.
A question for you

So, that is my day. It is busy, but I like it. Now I have some questions for you. What time do you get up? What do you eat for breakfast? How do you go to school or to work? What time do you go to bed? Do you always brush your teeth two times a day? Write your answers in English. Use words like always, usually, often, sometimes, and never. They are very useful words.
Here are my answers one more time. I always get up at half past six. I usually walk to school. I often eat cereal. I sometimes take the bus. I never go to bed after ten o'clock. And you?

Here is a small tip from Ms. Hill, my teacher. She says, "Talk about your day in English every night. It takes only two minutes." So every night, before I sleep, I say three sentences to Lucky. For example: "Today I got up early. I had pizza for lunch. I was very tired after soccer." Lucky never answers, but she always listens. Try it tonight!

items.title: Shopping at the Supermarket
items.summary: 跟着麦克斯和妈妈逛一次超市：水果蔬菜、肉和奶、价格、找零。把购物时最常用的词和问句都放进去。
paras: Hi! I am Max. I am ten years old. Every Saturday morning, I go shopping with my mom. We go to the big supermarket near our house. It is called Fresh Mart. I like going to the supermarket, because I can help my mom, and sometimes she buys me a treat. Today I want to take you shopping with us. Let's go!
Making a list
Before we go, we always make a shopping list. My mom says, "No list, no shopping." A list helps us remember everything. It also helps us save money, because we do not buy things we do not need.

We sit at the kitchen table. Mom opens the fridge. She looks inside and says, "We need some milk and two bags of apples." I write it down. Then she opens the cupboard. "We need rice, pasta, and a box of cereal." I write it down. Then she looks at the bread box. It is empty. "And a loaf of bread," she says. I write that down too.
Here is our list for today:
Milk, apples, bananas, tomatoes, potatoes, onions, chicken, fish, eggs, cheese, bread, rice, pasta, cereal, orange juice, and toothpaste.
It is a long list. I put the list in my pocket, and we get in the car.
Getting a cart

At the supermarket, the first thing we do is get a cart. The carts are outside, next to the door. Some carts are big, and some carts are small. We always take a big one. One wheel on our cart is often a little broken. It goes "squeak, squeak, squeak" all the way around the store. My mom laughs and says, "We have a singing cart today."

When we walk in, the doors open by themselves. The supermarket is very big and very bright. There is music in the air. There are many people. Some people are fast, and some people are slow. Some people are talking on their phones. A little baby is crying in one cart. A man is looking at his list with a confused face.
The fruit and vegetables

The first part of the store is the fruit and vegetables. Everything is fresh and colorful. There are red apples, green apples, and yellow apples. There are bananas, oranges, grapes, pears, peaches, and big round watermelons. On the other side, there are vegetables. There are tomatoes, potatoes, onions, carrots, lettuce, cucumbers, and broccoli.

"Max, please get two bags of apples," says Mom. I take a plastic bag and put six apples in it. Then I take another bag and put six more apples in it. I check them carefully. A good apple is hard and shiny. A bad apple is soft and has brown spots.
"I want an orange and a banana," I say. "For my lunch box."
"Okay," says Mom. "Get a bunch of bananas. Not one banana, a bunch."
A bunch of bananas has five or six bananas together. I find a nice bunch. They are yellow with a little green at the top. "Green is good," says Mom. "They will be ready in two days."
Then we get tomatoes, potatoes, and onions. The potatoes are in a big brown bag. The bag is very heavy. "How many potatoes are in this bag?" I ask.
Mom looks at the label. "It says five pounds. Maybe fifteen or twenty potatoes."
"That is a lot of potatoes," I say.
"Your dad loves potatoes," she says. "He eats them every day."
Reading prices
Every food in the supermarket has a price. The price is on a small sign under the food. Mom says I must always look at the price. Some things are cheap, and some things are expensive.
"Max, how much are the tomatoes?" Mom asks.
I look at the sign. "Two dollars and fifty cents for one pound," I read.
"And how much are those tomatoes?" She points to a different box. The tomatoes in that box are smaller.
"One dollar and ninety-nine cents for one pound," I say.
"Good. Which is cheaper?"
"The small ones are cheaper," I say. "They are fifty-one cents cheaper."
"Great math!" says Mom. "We will get the small ones. They taste the same."

In America, money is in dollars and cents. One dollar is one hundred cents. We write two dollars and fifty cents like this: $2.50. A penny is one cent. A nickel is five cents. A dime is ten cents. A quarter is twenty-five cents. I like quarters the best, because they are big and shiny.
Meat and fish

Next, we go to the meat and fish part of the store. It is at the back. It is cold there. There is a big glass case with chicken, beef, pork, and fish. A man in a white hat works behind the case. He is the butcher.
"Good morning!" he says. "What would you like today?"
"I'd like two pounds of chicken, please," says Mom. "And one pound of salmon."
The butcher puts the chicken on a scale. The scale shows the weight. "Two point one pounds," he says. "Is that okay?"
"That is fine, thank you," says Mom.
He wraps the chicken in white paper. Then he gets the salmon. Salmon is a pink fish. It is good for your brain, my mom says. I am not sure about that, but I like it with rice and a little lemon.
The dairy aisle

A supermarket has many aisles. An aisle is a long way between two big shelves. Each aisle has a number and a sign. Aisle one is bread. Aisle two is cereal. Aisle three is rice and pasta. Aisle seven is dairy. Dairy means milk, cheese, butter, yogurt, and eggs.

We go to aisle seven. It is very cold, because all the food is in big fridges with glass doors. I open a door and take a gallon of milk. A gallon is very big. It is about four liters. Then I take a carton of eggs. A carton of eggs has twelve eggs. I open it and check every egg. "None of them are broken," I say. Mom smiles.

Then we look at the cheese. There are many kinds of cheese. There is yellow cheese, white cheese, cheese with holes, and very smelly cheese. A woman is standing next to a small table. She is giving people little pieces of cheese on toothpicks.
"Would you like a free sample?" she asks me.
"Yes, please!" I say. I take a piece. It is soft and a little salty. It is delicious.
"How much is this cheese?" Mom asks.
"It is five dollars and ninety-nine cents," says the woman. "But today it is on sale. It is only four dollars."
"Great," says Mom. "We will take one."

Sales are good. On sale means cheaper than the normal price. My mom loves sales. Every week, she looks at the supermarket's sale paper on her phone. She says, "Buy what is on sale, and cook what you buy."
Bread, rice, and cereal

Next, we go to aisle one for bread. There is white bread, brown bread, bread with seeds, and long French bread. Mom wants a loaf of brown bread. A loaf is one whole piece of bread before you cut it. I choose the loaf and put it on top of the other things, so it does not get squashed.

Then we go to aisle three. We get a bag of rice and two boxes of pasta. Then aisle two. Aisle two is my favorite aisle, because it has the cereal. There are hundreds of boxes. Some boxes have cartoon animals on them. Some boxes have toys inside.
"Can I choose the cereal?" I ask.
"You can choose," says Mom. "But it can't be the one with marshmallows."
I look for a long time. Finally, I choose a box of corn flakes with honey. It is not my favorite, but it is good. Mom says, "Good choice."
The frozen food

We need orange juice, so we go to the frozen food aisle. Frozen food is in very cold freezers. There is ice cream, frozen pizza, frozen vegetables, and frozen fish. My eyes go straight to the ice cream. There is chocolate, vanilla, strawberry, and mint chocolate chip.
"Mom," I say, "we do not need ice cream. But I think we want ice cream."
Mom laughs. "That is very honest. Okay. One small box. Because you helped me so much today."
I choose mint chocolate chip. It is the best flavor in the world.
The checkout

Now our cart is full. It is time to pay. We go to the front of the store. This part is called the checkout. There are many lines. Each line has a cashier. The cashier takes your food and tells you the price. Some lines are long, and some lines are short. We find a short line.
Our cashier is a young man with a friendly face. His name tag says "Tony." "Hi, how are you today?" he asks.
"Good, thanks," says Mom. "And you?"
"Great, thanks," says Tony.
I help Mom put all the food on the black belt. The belt moves, and Tony takes each thing. He scans it with a small red light. Beep. Beep. Beep. The price goes on a little screen.
"Do you have a store card?" he asks.
"Yes," says Mom. She gives him her card. With a store card, some things are cheaper.
When everything is scanned, Tony says, "Your total is sixty-three dollars and forty cents."
Mom gives him four twenty-dollar bills. That is eighty dollars. Tony gives her the change. "Sixteen dollars and sixty cents is your change," he says. "Have a great day!"
"Thank you. You too!" we say.

Then I help put the food in our bags. We bring our own bags from home. They are made of cloth, and we use them again and again. My mom says plastic bags are bad for the ocean. I put the heavy things, like milk and potatoes, at the bottom. I put the light things, like bread and eggs, on top.
Going home
We push our singing cart to the car. Squeak, squeak, squeak. We put the bags in the trunk. Then I return the cart to the cart area. My mom says, "Always return your cart. It is good manners."

At home, I help Mom put everything away. Milk, cheese, eggs, and chicken go in the fridge. The ice cream goes in the freezer. The apples and bananas go in a bowl on the table. The rice, pasta, and cereal go in the cupboard.
Then I take out my list from my pocket. I check every word. Milk, yes. Apples, yes. Bananas, yes. Tomatoes, yes. Toothpaste... Oh no! We forgot the toothpaste!
Mom looks at me. I look at Mom. Then we both laugh.
"Next Saturday," says Mom. "Write it at the top of the list."
Useful supermarket English
Here are some useful questions and sentences from today. You can use them in any supermarket:

Excuse me, where is the milk? It is in aisle seven. How much is this? It is three dollars. How many eggs are in a carton? There are twelve. Is this on sale? Yes, it is two for five dollars. I'd like one pound of chicken, please. Can I pay with a card? Yes, of course. Do you need a bag? No, thank you. I have my own bag. Where are the shopping carts? They are outside, next to the door. How many apples do you want? I want six, please.

Try this at home: write your own shopping list in English. Look in your fridge and in your cupboard. What do you need? Write the names of the food, and next to each one, write how much or how many. For example: two bottles of water, one bag of rice, a dozen eggs, some cheese. Then go to the store and read the prices. Which things are cheap? Which things are expensive? You will learn many new words, and maybe you will save some money too.

items.title: My Family and My Home
items.summary: 诺亚带你认识他的大家庭和房子：家庭成员称呼、外貌和性格、每个房间里有什么。家庭和住房类高频词一次学全。
paras: Hi! I am Noah. I am twelve years old. Today I want to tell you about two important things in my life: my family and my home. My family is big and loud, and my home is old and busy. I love them both. Come with me, and I will show you everything.
My family

There are seven people in my family. There is my dad, my mom, my big sister Emma, my little brothers Jack and Leo, my grandma, and me. We also have a dog called Pepper and two fish called Salt and Sugar. So, really, we have ten family members. My mom says ten is too many. My dad says ten is perfect.
My dad

My dad's name is David. He is forty-two years old. He is very tall. He is the tallest person in our family. He has brown hair and a short beard. He wears glasses, but only for reading. He works at a bank in the city. He gets up very early, and he comes home at six o'clock.

My dad is funny. He tells jokes at dinner every night. Most of his jokes are bad. For example: "Why did the cookie go to the doctor? Because it felt crummy!" We all say, "Oh, Dad!" But then we laugh, because his face is so happy. My dad likes cooking on the weekend. He makes very good pancakes on Sunday morning. He also likes fixing things in the house, but he is not very good at it. Last month, he fixed the kitchen light. Now the light turns on when we open the fridge. We do not know why.
My mom

My mom's name is Anna. She is thirty-nine years old. My mom is tall, and she has short black hair. She has brown eyes and a big smile. She is a teacher at a high school. She teaches math. She is very smart, and she is very organized. She has a big calendar on the kitchen wall. Everybody's plans are on the calendar. Doctor visits, soccer games, birthdays, and dentist visits. If it is not on the calendar, it does not happen.

My mom is kind, but she is also strict. She has many rules. No phones at the table. No shoes in the house. Homework before games. Bed at nine o'clock. My brothers and I sometimes complain about the rules, but secretly we think she is the best mom in the world.
My sister

My big sister Emma is sixteen. She has long brown hair and green eyes, like our grandma. She is quiet and very creative. She loves drawing and music. She plays the guitar in her room every evening. Sometimes she plays the same song fifty times. I can hear it through the wall. Emma is in high school. She wants to be an artist or a designer.

Emma is usually nice to me. She helps me with my English homework. But she does not like it when I go into her room. On her door, there is a sign. It says, "Knock first. No little brothers." I am her only little brother who can read, so I know that sign is for me.
My little brothers

Jack and Leo are twins. They are six years old. Twins are two babies born on the same day from the same mom. Jack and Leo look almost the same. They both have curly blond hair and blue eyes. They are both short and full of energy. Many people cannot tell them apart. But I can. Jack has a small scar on his chin. He fell off his bike last year. And Leo has a missing front tooth.

The twins are very loud. They run everywhere. They never walk. They jump on the sofa, they jump on the beds, and once they jumped into the pool with their clothes on. My mom says they have the energy of ten small dogs. They are also very funny. They tell their own jokes. Their jokes are even worse than Dad's jokes.
My grandma

My grandma lives with us. She is my mom's mother. She is seventy-four years old. She has short white hair and kind green eyes. She wears big round glasses and colorful sweaters. Grandma is very good at many things. She can knit, she can bake bread, she can grow tomatoes, and she can win any card game. She always wins. I think she cheats, but I cannot prove it.

Grandma tells us stories about the old days. When she was young, there were no phones and no computers. She walked two miles to school every day. "In the snow," she says. "Uphill. Both ways." I am not sure that is possible, but it is a good story.
My other family

I also have a big family outside our house. My dad has two brothers. They are my uncles, Uncle Mike and Uncle Tom. My mom has one sister. She is my aunt, Aunt Lisa. Uncle Mike and his wife have three children. They are my cousins. My cousins are about the same age as me, and we play video games together on holidays. My grandpa, my dad's father, lives in another state. My grandpa has got a long white beard. He looks like Santa Claus. Every December, little children at the mall ask him for presents.

My mom's parents are my grandparents too. My grandma lives with us, but my grandpa on my mom's side died before I was born. Grandma keeps his photo on a small table next to the lamp in her room. She says I have his smile. Aunt Lisa has a new baby. The baby's name is Rose, and she is only three months old. She sleeps, she eats, and she cries. Everybody wants to hold her.

At Thanksgiving, my whole family comes to our house. There are about twenty-five people. We need three tables, and the kitchen is very hot. Everybody talks at the same time. It is very noisy, but it is my favorite day of the year.
My home

Now let me show you my home. We live in a big old house on Maple Street. The house is white with a green door. It is about one hundred years old. It has two floors, a basement, and a small garden. The floors make noises when you walk. Grandma says the house is talking. The twins say there is a ghost.
The living room

When you open the green door, you are in the hallway. On the left, there is the living room. In the living room, there is a big gray sofa. It is very soft and very old. There are two armchairs, a coffee table, and a big TV on the wall. Next to the TV, there is a tall shelf with books, games, and family photos. There is a photo of my parents on their wedding day. My dad has lots of hair in that photo.

There is also a fireplace in the living room. In winter, we make a fire, and everybody sits on the sofa. Pepper the dog lies on the carpet in front of the fire. That is her favorite place in the whole house.
The kitchen

On the right side of the hallway, there is the kitchen. The kitchen is the busiest room in our house. It is big and yellow. There is a long wooden table in the middle with eight chairs. There is a fridge, an oven, a microwave, and a dishwasher. On the fridge, there are many magnets and many pictures. Most of the pictures are by the twins. They are pictures of dinosaurs, rockets, and Pepper.

Grandma spends a lot of time in the kitchen. She bakes bread on Monday and cookies on Friday. The kitchen always smells good. The fish tank is in the kitchen too, on a small table next to the window. Salt and Sugar swim around and around. They are orange and white. They do not do much, but they are very relaxing to watch.
Upstairs
From the hallway, the stairs go up to the second floor. There are fourteen stairs. I know, because the twins count them every day. Upstairs, there are four bedrooms and two bathrooms.

The first bedroom is the biggest. This is my parents' bedroom. It has a big bed, two closets, and a big window. We are not allowed to jump on their bed. The twins jump on it anyway when Mom is not home.

The second bedroom is Emma's room. Her walls are dark blue, and she has posters of bands and paintings everywhere. She has a desk, a bed, a guitar, and many plants. Her room is always clean. Mine is not.

The third bedroom is Grandma's room. It is small and warm. She has a rocking chair next to the window. She sits there and knits in the afternoon. There are photos of all her grandchildren on the wall. She has eleven grandchildren.

The fourth bedroom is mine. But I do not have it alone. I share it with the twins. There are three beds in our room. My bed is next to the window. The twins have bunk beds. Jack sleeps on the top bed, and Leo sleeps on the bottom bed. Every night they fight about it, and every night Leo loses.

Sharing a room with twins is not easy. They wake up very early, at six o'clock, even on Saturday. They talk all the time. They take my things. Last week, Leo used my soccer socks as puppets. But sometimes it is nice. At night, when the lights are off, we tell each other stories. Sometimes the stories are scary, and the twins climb into my bed. Then all three of us sleep in one small bed. It is not comfortable, but it is warm.
The bathrooms

There are two bathrooms upstairs. One is for my parents and Grandma. The other one is for us four kids. Four kids and one bathroom is a big problem in the morning. Emma takes thirty minutes in the shower. The twins splash water everywhere. I always have to wait. My dad says, "In a big family, you learn to be patient." I say, "In a big family, you learn to get up first."
The basement and the garage

Under the house, there is a basement. It is dark and a little scary. There is a washing machine, a dryer, and lots of old boxes. My dad's tools are down there too. Next to the house, there is a garage. Our car is in the garage, and our bikes are there too. There is also a ping-pong table. On rainy days, we play ping-pong for hours.
The garden

Behind the house, there is a small garden. Grandma grows tomatoes, carrots, and flowers there. There is a big tree in the corner with a swing. The twins love the swing. There is also a small wooden house for Pepper, but she never sleeps in it. She sleeps inside, on the sofa, when nobody is looking.

Our neighbors are the Garcias. Their house is small, but their garden is big. They have chickens! Every week, Mrs. Garcia gives us a box of fresh eggs, and Grandma gives her a loaf of bread. That is a good trade.
Why I love my home

My home is not new. Some windows do not close well. The stairs make noise. The kitchen light is still a little strange. But my home is full of people I love. There is always someone to talk to, someone to play with, and someone to eat with. When I come home from school, I hear the guitar from Emma's room, I smell Grandma's bread, and I hear the twins laughing. Then Pepper runs to the door and jumps on me. That is when I know I am home.

Now it is your turn. Who is in your family? What do they look like? What is your home like? How many rooms are there? Do you share your bedroom? Try to write ten sentences in English about your family and your home.

items.title: Weather, Seasons, and What to Wear
items.summary: 从春夏秋冬四个季节讲天气、温度和衣服，再加上天气预报的常用说法。适合学天气和服装类高频词。
paras: Hello, everybody! My name is Mia, and I love the weather. Some people think weather is boring. They only say, "Nice day today," and that is all. But I think weather is very interesting. Every day is different. One day is sunny, the next day is rainy, and sometimes there is a big storm with thunder and lightning. Weather changes what we wear, what we eat, and what we do. In this article, I will tell you about the weather and the four seasons, and about the clothes we wear in each season.
What is the weather like today?
When people talk about the weather in English, they usually start with "It is." For example: It is sunny. It is cloudy. It is rainy. It is windy. It is snowy. It is foggy. It is hot. It is cold.
We also use "It is" with a verb ending in -ing. Look outside! It is snowing! It is raining. It is getting dark. This means the weather is happening right now.

Let me look out of my window. What is the weather like today? It is sunny and warm today. The sky is blue, and there are only two small white clouds. There is a little wind, so the leaves on the tree are moving. It is a perfect day to go to the park.
How hot? How cold?

We use temperature to say how hot or cold it is. In the United States, people use Fahrenheit. In most other countries, people use Celsius. When I talk to my cousin in Canada, we always get confused. I say, "It is seventy degrees today!" and she says, "Seventy? You must be on fire!" Because seventy degrees Fahrenheit is about twenty-one degrees Celsius. That is warm, but not hot.

Here are some temperatures in both. Thirty-two degrees Fahrenheit is zero degrees Celsius. Water turns to ice. Fifty degrees Fahrenheit is ten degrees Celsius. That is cool. You need a jacket. Seventy degrees Fahrenheit is about twenty-one degrees Celsius. That is warm and nice. Ninety degrees Fahrenheit is about thirty-two degrees Celsius. That is hot. One hundred degrees Fahrenheit is about thirty-eight degrees Celsius. That is very, very hot. Stay inside!

We have special words for different temperatures. From cold to hot, they are: freezing, cold, cool, warm, hot, and boiling. "Freezing" means very, very cold. "Boiling" means very, very hot. My dad always says "boiling" in the summer, and he always says "freezing" in the winter. My mom says he is never happy with the weather.
Spring
There are four seasons in a year: spring, summer, fall, and winter. In many countries, fall is also called autumn.

Spring is in March, April, and May. In spring, the weather starts to get warmer. The days get longer. The snow melts, and the grass turns green again. Flowers come out. Birds come back from the south and sing in the trees every morning. Baby animals are born. Spring is a time of new life.

But spring weather can be crazy. In the morning, it is sunny. At lunch time, it is cloudy. In the afternoon, it is raining. Then the sun comes out again. In spring, you often need an umbrella in your bag. My grandma says, "April showers bring May flowers." A shower is a short rain. So she means the rain in April helps the flowers grow in May.

What do I wear in spring? I wear jeans, a long-sleeve shirt, and a light jacket. When it rains, I wear my yellow raincoat and my red rain boots. I love my rain boots, because I can jump in puddles. A puddle is a little pool of water on the ground after the rain. Jumping in puddles is one of the best things about spring.
Summer

Summer is in June, July, and August. Summer is the hottest season of the year. The sun is strong, and the days are very long. In June, it is still light outside at nine o'clock at night. There is no school in summer, so children are very happy.

In summer, the weather is usually sunny and hot. Sometimes it is very humid. Humid means the air is wet and heavy. When it is humid, you feel sticky all day. Sometimes there are big summer storms. The sky gets dark very fast. There is thunder, a loud BOOM in the sky. There is lightning, a bright light in the sky. Then there is heavy rain for twenty minutes. After the storm, the air is cool and fresh, and sometimes you can see a rainbow.

When it is hot, I wear shorts and a T-shirt. I wear sandals on my feet. I always wear a hat and sunglasses outside. And my mom always says, "Don't forget your sunscreen!" Sunscreen is a cream you put on your skin. It stops the sun from burning you. You should wear a hat and sunscreen when you are outside in summer. I forgot my sunscreen one time at the beach. My face was as red as a tomato for three days.

What do we do in summer? We go to the beach. We swim in the pool. We eat ice cream and watermelon. We have barbecues in the garden. At night, we sit outside and look at the stars. Summer is my brother's favorite season.
Fall

Fall is in September, October, and November. In fall, the weather starts to get cooler. The days get shorter. The leaves on the trees change color. They turn yellow, orange, red, and brown. Then they fall down from the trees. That is why this season is called "fall." The ground is covered with leaves. My dad uses a rake to put the leaves in a big pile, and my little sister and I jump into the pile. Then my dad has to do it again.

Fall weather is often windy. Sometimes it is foggy in the morning. Fog is like a cloud on the ground. When it is foggy, you can't see very far. Cars must drive slowly. In late fall, it can be cold and rainy.

In fall, I wear long pants and a sweater. In the morning, it is cool, so I wear a jacket. In the afternoon, it is warmer, so I take my jacket off. Then I forget my jacket at school. My mom says I have forgotten twelve jackets at school. That is not true. It is only ten.

What do we do in fall? We go back to school. We pick apples at a farm. We make pumpkin pie. At the end of October, there is Halloween. Children wear costumes and go from house to house. They say, "Trick or treat!" and people give them candy. Fall is my favorite season, because I love the colors and I love candy.
Winter

Winter is in December, January, and February. Winter is the coldest season of the year. The days are very short. It gets dark at five o'clock in the afternoon. In many places, it snows in winter. Snow is white and soft. It falls from the sky like little white stars. When it snows a lot, everything is white. The trees, the houses, the cars, and the streets.

When it snows a lot, sometimes there is no school. That is called a snow day. On a snow day, we stay home and play in the snow. We build a snowman with a carrot nose. We have snowball fights. We go sledding on the hill. Then we come inside and drink hot chocolate. Snow days are the best days of the year.

But winter can be difficult too. The roads are icy, and it is dangerous to drive. Some days it is freezing, and the wind is very cold. My fingers and my nose get red. In some places, there are big snowstorms called blizzards. In a blizzard, there is a lot of snow and a very strong wind.

When it is cold, I wear a lot of clothes. I wear a warm coat, a sweater, a scarf, a hat, gloves, and boots. My mom says, "Wear layers." Layers means many clothes, one on top of another. A T-shirt, then a long-sleeve shirt, then a sweater, then a coat. When you are hot, you can take one layer off. In winter, I look like a big round ball with a small face.

What do we do in winter? We go ice skating. We read books next to the fire. We make cookies. In December, there are many holidays. My family celebrates Christmas, and my friend Sam celebrates Hanukkah. On December 31st, we stay up late and say, "Happy New Year!" at midnight.
The weather forecast

Every morning, my dad checks the weather forecast. A weather forecast tells us about the weather tomorrow or next week. The person on TV who tells the forecast is called a weather reporter. Our weather reporter is a man named Bob. He always wears a colorful tie, and he always smiles, even when the weather is terrible.

Here is a typical forecast from Bob: "Good morning! Today it will be sunny with a high of seventy-five degrees. Tonight it will be clear and cool, with a low of fifty-five. Tomorrow it will be cloudy, and it will rain in the afternoon. On the weekend, it will be windy and cold. Don't forget your umbrella!"

A "high" is the hottest temperature in the day. A "low" is the coldest temperature, usually at night. When the forecast says "a chance of rain," it means maybe it will rain, and maybe it will not. My dad says Bob is right about half the time. My mom says that is better than Dad.
Weather in different places

The weather is different all around the world. In some places, it is hot all year. In other places, it is cold all year. In the desert, it is very hot and dry in the day, but cold at night. In the rainforest, it is hot and it rains almost every day. At the North Pole, it is freezing all year, and the sun does not come up for months in winter.

In southern California, where my uncle lives, the weather is sunny almost every day. It does not snow there, except on the tall mountains. In summer, it can be very hot, more than one hundred degrees. My uncle says, "We have two seasons in California: summer and a little less summer."
In London, where my aunt lives, it rains a lot. She says she always carries an umbrella, even on sunny days. Because in London, a sunny morning can quickly become a rainy afternoon.
Why weather is important

Weather is not only about clothes. Weather is important for many people. Farmers need rain for their plants. Pilots need good weather to fly. Fishermen need calm weather to go out on the sea. Truck drivers need to know about snow and ice on the roads. And children need to know if there is a snow day tomorrow!
Weather words to remember
Let us review. Here are some sentences to practice. Read them out loud.

What is the weather like today? It is sunny and hot. What is the weather like in winter? It is cold and snowy. What is the temperature? It is sixty-five degrees. Is it raining? Yes, it is. Take your umbrella. What should I wear? It is cold, so you should wear a coat and gloves. What is your favorite season? My favorite season is fall, because I love the colors.

Now look out of your window. What is the weather like where you are? What are you wearing today? Write five sentences about the weather today. Then check the forecast and write three sentences about the weather tomorrow. You can be a weather reporter, just like Bob. Just don't forget the colorful tie!

One last tip from me: talk about the weather with people around you. In English-speaking countries, the weather is the most popular small talk. Say "Beautiful day, isn't it?" or "Cold today, huh?" to a neighbor or a cashier. It is an easy way to practice, and people always answer.
